{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-in-s","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"e012a57b6bece26309c94d983a03a8c1504409218a86e8266728b584e2dcff89","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-in-class-std:lineage:37","source_registry_sha256":"2800087d52ca58455ac6dac735a6e1bd60a4442f9e09c2356d96bd9ed8102504","source_liveness_sha256":"4d2b75b9a10fb774f53fb2d906a3a7a7f75f5e9387f8b4ddcd423e9b7828d59b"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Accidents and emergency situations: duties after a crash, avoiding collisions, water and shoulder emergencies, impaired driving, roadside emergencies, equipment failures, theft, traffic stops and carbon monoxide","heading":"C — Duties at a crash scene, proof of insurance after a crash, collision avoidance choices, leaving the pavement, a car in water, alcohol and drugs, spotting impaired drivers, roadside safety, blowouts, brake failure, ignition lock, theft prevention, traffic stops and carbon monoxide","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Duties at a crash scene, proof of insurance after a crash, collision avoidance choices, leaving the pavement, a car in water, alcohol and drugs, spotting impaired drivers, roadside safety, blowouts, brake failure, ignition lock, theft prevention, traffic stops and carbon monoxide
Knowledge domain: what Indiana requires of a driver after a crash, how to choose among stopping, turning and speeding up to avoid a collision, what to do when the car leaves the pavement or goes into water, how alcohol and drugs impair driving and how to spot an impaired driver, how to handle a roadside breakdown, a blowout, brake failure and the ignition lock, how to reduce theft, how to behave during a traffic stop, and how to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning.

FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A01
Failure to yield the right of way is the most common factor among all collisions in Indiana. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A01
A driver involved in a crash must stop immediately, or as close to the scene as possible without blocking traffic more than necessary. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A01
If the crash happens on the traveled part of a highway, the driver must move the vehicle off the highway near the scene, unless the crash involves hazardous materials or causes injury, death or entrapment. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A01
A driver must stay at the crash scene, give their name, address and vehicle registration number to everyone involved, and show their driver's license. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A01
When a crash injures or kills someone, the driver must give reasonable help to people hurt or trapped as directed by police, medical staff or a 911 operator, and should make sure police are notified as soon as possible. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A01
After hitting an unattended vehicle or other property, stop, stay at the scene, try to notify the owner, and call police with the information if the owner cannot be found. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A01
After a crash, if the BMV asks, your insurer must electronically file a Certificate of Compliance showing you had at least the state minimum liability coverage at the time. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A01
To avoid a collision you can stop quickly, turn quickly away from the danger if you cannot stop in time, or speed up when accelerating is the best or only way out. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A01
If a crash looks likely, steer away from oncoming traffic even if that means leaving the road, and drive off the road rather than skidding off. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A01
If you must hit something, pick something that gives way, like brush, over something hard, and a vehicle moving your way over a still object, but a still object is safer than a head-on crash. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A02
If your wheels drift onto the shoulder, do not jerk back onto the pavement; drive along the shoulder, ease off the gas and steer back gradually after slowing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A02
A car that plunges into water usually floats for several minutes, giving occupants time to escape through an open window while it is still on the surface. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A02
In a car in water, do not try to open a door, because water pressure makes it nearly impossible and an open door floods the inside. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A02
In a car in water, remove your seat belt, open a window, free children from restraints, climb out onto the roof and call 911, and never go back in for belongings. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A02
Alcohol harms clear thinking and physical coordination and slows reaction time, and blood alcohol concentration depends mainly on how much is drunk, how fast and the person's body weight. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A02
Many prescription, over-the-counter and recreational drugs impair reasoning and coordination, so check the label and ask a physician or pharmacist about side effects before driving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A02
Signs of a possibly impaired driver include wide turns, straddling the center line or weaving, unusual speed, near misses, stopping for no reason, and driving at night without headlights. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A03
In a roadside emergency, pull onto the shoulder if you can and turn on your hazard lights. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A03
Place a red emergency reflective triangle 200 feet behind your vehicle, or 500 feet behind it on a hill or curve. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A03
If you have to get out on a roadside shoulder, exit on the passenger side after checking for traffic, obstructions and drop-offs. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A03
In a blowout, hold the wheel firmly, keep going straight, take your foot off the gas without braking, and brake only when the car is almost stopped off the road. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A03
If conventional brakes fail, move to a lower gear when you can, then press the brake pedal hard and fast a few times to build up pressure. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A03
When using the parking brake after a brake failure, hold the release so you can let go if the rear wheels lock, and once stopped, call for help rather than driving on. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A03
Never turn the ignition to the lock position while moving in a car with a steering wheel interlock, because the steering will lock and you will lose control. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A03
To reduce theft, take the keys, lock the doors, never hide a spare key in or near the car, never leave it running unattended, and park in well-lit, patrolled areas. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A03
When police signal you to stop, turn on your right turn signal to show you have seen the officer. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A04
Pull over to the right shoulder, never into the center median or the opposite side of a two-lane road, and if there is no safe shoulder slow down with hazards on until you find a safe place. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec09-F28 | anchor: A04
During a traffic stop, stay inside the vehicle unless the officer tells you to get out, end phone calls and turn off the radio. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec09-F29 | anchor: A04
During a traffic stop, keep hands in view, the driver's on the steering wheel and passengers' on their laps, and tell the officer where documents are before reaching for them. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec09-F30 | anchor: A04
Signing a traffic ticket is not an admission of guilt, only an acknowledgment that you received it, and any dispute belongs in traffic court rather than at the roadside. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec09-F31 | anchor: A05
Carbon monoxide cannot be seen, smelled or tasted, and it is most likely to enter a vehicle when the heater is on, the exhaust system is faulty, or in heavy traffic. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec09-F32 | anchor: A05
Never run a vehicle's engine in a closed garage, and close the fresh-air vent in congested traffic but open it on highways in cold weather. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0067]

Misconceptions: you do not always leave the car where it stopped, a crash on the traveled highway must be moved off unless hazardous materials, injury, death or entrapment are involved; opening a door is the wrong escape from a car in water, the window is the way out; braking hard in a blowout is wrong, ease off the gas first; signing a ticket does not admit guilt.
Mnemonics: stop, turn or speed up to avoid a crash; belt off, window open, kids out, onto the roof; right signal, right shoulder, stay inside, hands in sight at a traffic stop; carbon monoxide is invisible, odorless and tasteless.
Glossary: Certificate of Compliance means the insurer's electronic proof of coverage sent to the BMV; entrapment means a person trapped in a vehicle; steering wheel interlock means a system that locks the steering when the ignition is switched to lock; carbon monoxide means a poisonous, invisible exhaust gas.
Dynamic facts: none in these pages; there are no fees, phone numbers or service details.
